new_statements.quote: Underlyingly, Blanga has no heavy syllables and displays the canonical Oceanic (Lynch et al. 2002:35) penultimate pattern, as is unequivocally revealed in list elicitation with multiple consultants of different ages and sexes. [...] List elicitations of quotation forms of underived words and frozen derivations with different numbers of syllables show that Blanga main stress is invariably penultimate: ˈi.fu ‘blow’, ˈsu.a ‘child’, ˈba.kɔ ‘cheek’, ˈɡra.fi ‘evening’, ˈzi.fla ‘exit’, dɔ.ˈve.le ‘tuber’, ma.za.ˈɣa.ni ‘be.young’, fu.fu.ɣɔ.ˈɡa.e ‘morning’.
new_statements.citation: Voica, Radu. 2020. Surface processes, word minimality and stress assignment in Blanga. JSEALS 13.2: 43-68 (Northern Blanga data; Zazao [jaj] identified as Southwestern/Zazao Blanga dialect of the same language, Blablanga blab1237).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (26 pp., text, the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Surface Processes, Word Minimality and Stress Assignment in Blanga'). Both halves of the quote are present verbatim: p.2 = printed p.44, sec. 1.1 'A matter of stress', paragraph 2: 'Underlyingly, Blanga has no heavy syllables and displays the canonical Oceanic (Lynch et al. 2002:35) penultimate pattern, as is unequivocally revealed in list elicitation with multiple consultants of different ages and sexes.' p.16 = printed p.58, sec. 4.1 'Analysis of underlying forms' (the compiler locator says 'sec. 4'; it is the 4.1 subsection): 'List elicitations of quotation forms of underived words and frozen deriv…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress on the penultimate syllable of the underlying (all-light-syllable) word, assigned by syllabic trochees built right-to-left with End Rule Right. Surface processes after stress assignment (diphthong formation, vowel coalescence, vowel deletion) can make the final syllable heavy and then stress appears on that final syllable (e.g. /ˈda.ta.u/ > [da.ˈtau]); Voica analyses this as preservation of the underlying trochaic structure, not as weight-sensitivity.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Rhythmic: alternating trochaic feet leftward from the penult give secondary stress on alternate preceding syllables; in compounds with an odd-syllable second element the secondary stress stays on the first syllable of the first element (e.g. /ˌka.la meˈmeha/, p. 65).
new_statements.exceptions: Surface final stress when the final syllable becomes heavy (diphthong/coalescence/syncope). Pijin loanwords may retain source stress (ˈsa.ra.re 'Saturday') and final-vowel epenthesis yields irregular antepenultimate stress (ˈle.mɔ.ne 'lemon', ˈpetrɔlɔ 'petrol') (p. 66). Loans from Cheke Holo and other Isabel languages conform to the penultimate pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, quotation (citation) forms from list elicitation of underived words and frozen derivations, multiple consultants; fieldwork 2009-2019. Data are from NORTHERN Blanga exclusively (p. 45); the Zazao/Kilokaka (Southwestern Blanga) dialect is not itself analysed, so the reading applies to zaza1245 only via the source's own identification of Zazao as a dialect of Blanga.
new_statements.identity_note: Zazao [jaj] is the communalect of Kilokaka village. Both field linguists who have worked on Isabel treat it as a dialect of Blablanga/Blanga [blp] = Glottolog blab1237, not a separate language: Palmer 1999: 9-10 (§1.6.2 'Rethinking Blablanga and Zazao': speakers of both 'claim they are variants of the same language'; 'Zazao' is a region name 'not used by speakers to refer to any of the three dialects'; Tryon & Hackman's 78.6% rests on the pre-1915 Napu list) and Voica 2020: 44-45 ('Southwestern Blanga or Zazao Blanga, again with about 500 speakers, is spoken in Kilokaka, Gazuhungari, Gugugluro, Kotlomuro, Galili (Fizaghalia), Hiroleghu, Biraki and Tavol.. Kilokaka was previously considered a different language and consequently assigned a different iso 639-3 code (jaj)'). The quoted stress statement is for Northern (Loghahaza) Blanga only ('The analysis in this article is based on data from Northern Blanga exclusively', p. 45). Recommended catalog handling: record zaza1245 as a dialect pointer to blab1237 carrying Voica 2020's statement, rather than as an independent Zazao datum; Voica's 2017 thesis (languages blp + jaj) is the place a Zazao-specific confirmation would be found.

new_statements.quote: List elicitations of quotation forms of underived words and frozen derivations with different numbers of syllables show that Blanga main stress is invariably penultimate: ˈi.fu ‘blow’, ˈsu.a ‘child’, ˈba.kɔ ‘cheek’, ˈɡra.fi ‘evening’, ˈzi.fla ‘exit’, dɔ.ˈve.le ‘tuber’, ma.za.ˈɣa.ni ‘be.young’, fu.fu.ɣɔ.ˈɡa.e ‘morning’. However, diphthong formation (2.1.7.2) and vowel deletion (2.1.6) can generate words with final stress at the surface. [p. 127] ... Underlying Blanga words are stressed on the penultimate syllable. [...] When the vowel of the underlyingly stressed syllable becomes V1 of the surface diphthong, words with final stress are generated. [...] Blanga employs syllabic trochees constructed from right to left and main stress is assigned to the head of the rightmost foot. [p. 138]

new_statements.relation_note: Same penultimate placement, essentially the same wording as the Voica 2020 existing statement (which is drawn from this thesis). The thesis states on p. 26 'This thesis deals exclusively with the northern variety', so, like Voica 2020, the stress statement is for Northern (Loghahaza) Blanga, not for Zazao/Kilokaka (Southwestern Blanga) specifically; it adds the identity ruling that Kilokaka/Zazao is a Blanga dialect (84.84% cognation, pp. 39-40: 'Kilokaka speakers sometimes refer to their dialect as Zazao Blanga'). No Zazao-specific stress datum anywhere in the thesis.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress on the penultimate syllable of the underlying (phonological) word; feet are syllabic trochees built right-to-left with End Rule Right, no weight sensitivity underlyingly (all syllables light). Surface final stress arises only when the penultimate vowel becomes the first element of a surface diphthong (/da.ˈta.u/ -> [da.ˈtau]); final-vowel deletion does not move stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the head of each non-final trochee (odd-syllabled words leave an unfooted initial syllable); compounds and full reduplications are 'phonologically right strong', with secondary stress on the first element (e.g. /`ka.la meˈmeha/ 'feather', /`va.ka ˈfla.lɔ/ 'airplane'), pp. 136-137.
new_statements.exceptions: Surface final stress after diphthong formation ([da.ˈtau] 'chief', [hna.pu.ˈɡai] 'morning'); heavy suffix -lau attracts stress ([a.re.ˈlau]) while light suffix -hi is analysed as extrametrical ([ˈa.ra.hi]); prefixes and echo syllables do not affect main stress (na.ˈfri.hŋe, fa.ka.ˈkra.ŋɔ). Stress is not contrastive; length is the main phonetic correlate (2.6.3.1), pending perception tests.
new_statements.identity_note: Voica's thesis (p. 26, p. 27) 'deals exclusively with the northern variety' of Blanga (Popoheo, Kolosori; also called Loghahaza Blanga). Zazao [jaj] = the Kilokaka communalect, which the thesis establishes as Southwestern (SW) Blanga, a dialect of Blanga/Blablanga [blab1237] (p. 40: 'Kilokaka speakers sometimes refer to their dialect as Zazao Blanga, Zazao being their own old settlement on the southern slopes'; 84.84% cognation with N Blanga, p. 39; 'Mention of the southern varieties will be made sporadically and mainly for comparison's sake', p. 26). So every stress statement available for zaza1245 is a statement about Northern Blanga transferred to Zazao via the dialect ruling; the only Zazao-specific description in print (Ray 1926: 532-534, from Napu's vocabulary) has no accent information.

new_statements.relation_note: No catalog record for zaza1245 (in_catalog false). The statement is the very source of existing_statements[1] (same thesis, same p. 127 wording) and matches existing_statements[0] (Voica 2020 JSEALS): fixed penultimate. It applies to Zazao only through the dialect identification (Zazao = SW Blanga, p. 40); the thesis data are Northern Blanga.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Underlying word stress in Blanga is fixed on the penultimate syllable (syllabic trochees built right to left, main stress on the head of the rightmost foot; no underlying heavy syllables). Surface diphthong formation can yield apparent final stress when the stressed vowel becomes V1 of a surface diphthong, and word-final vowel deletion yields CVC finals that do not attract stress; neither alters the penultimate pattern. The thesis describes Northern Blanga only ('This thesis deals exclusively with the northern variety', p. 26) and identifies Zazao/Kilokaka as Southwestern Blanga, a dialect of the same language (p. 40); it gives no Zazao-specific stress data.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Trochaic alternation right to left gives secondary stresses on alternate syllables leftward of the main stress; in compounds with an odd-syllabled second element the secondary stress stays on the first syllable of the first element (e.g. /`ka.la meˈmeha/), so compounds and full reduplications are footed as separate phonological words at a layer above the word (sec. 2.6.3.3.6, pp. 136-137).
new_statements.exceptions: Surface final stress from diphthong formation when the underlyingly stressed vowel becomes V1 of the diphthong; surface CVC syllables from word-final vowel deletion do not attract stress (p. 138); a word-final heavy syllable forms a proper syllabic trochee (Hayes 1995 prediction, p. 128); loanword stress treated in sec. 2.7.
new_statements.identity_note: Voica 2017 describes Northern (Loghahaza) Blanga, villages Popoheo and Kolosori, Santa Isabel ('This thesis deals exclusively with the northern variety', p. 26); Zazao [jaj] is identified as Southwestern (Zazao) Blanga spoken in and around Kilokaka, one of three slightly different Blanga dialects (p. 40; cognation with N Blanga 84.84%). No stress data specific to the Zazao dialect are given.
